name: What is the difference between a second-story addition and a pop-top?

mainEntity.name: How is a full second-story addition different from a pop-top remodel, and which one is usually more practical in Los Angeles?
mainEntity.text: How is a full second-story addition different from a pop-top remodel, and which one is usually more practical in Los Angeles?

acceptedAnswer.text: A second-story addition and a pop-top are related but not identical. A second-story addition usually refers to adding an entire new upper floor over much or all of the existing home. A pop-top is often used when only part of the roof and upper structure is replaced or expanded, which can reduce demolition and sometimes lower cost. However, a pop-top is not automatically simpler. The existing framing, roof geometry, setbacks, height limits, and structural capacity can make a partial upper addition just as complex as a full second story. In dense neighborhoods around Los Angeles, Glendale, Pasadena, and Burbank, the right choice depends on lot constraints, neighborhood character, and budget. Homeowners often consider a pop-top when they want to preserve part of the first-floor structure or minimize demo, but a full second story may produce a cleaner layout and better long-term value. The decision should be based on structural feasibility, not just terminology.
acceptedAnswer.description: A second-story addition usually means building a full new upper level, while a pop-top typically keeps part of the existing structure and adds a lighter upper expansion. Pop-tops can be less expensive and disruptive, but they are not always structurally or architecturally feasible for every house.
